nameStory: Wright viburnum is named after Charles Wright, a 19th-century American botanist who collected plants across Asia and North America for Harvard University. This Asian native earned its scientific honor through Wright's dedicated plant collecting expeditions in Japan and other parts of East Asia in the 1850s.
description: Wright viburnum is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall and wide, forming a rounded, somewhat open shape. This Asian ornamental produces clusters of small white flowers in late spring, followed by bright red berries that mature to black in fall. The oval leaves have prominent veining and turn attractive shades of red and purple in autumn, making it a popular landscape choice in New England gardens.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to egg-shaped leaves are 2-4 inches long with prominent parallel veins running from the midrib to the leaf edges, creating a distinctly ribbed texture you can feel with your fingertips

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers appear in flat-topped clusters 3-4 inches across in late May to early June, with a sweet, subtle fragrance that attracts bees and other pollinators

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries in late summer gradually ripen to glossy black by fall, hanging in drooping clusters that birds eagerly consume

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a rounded shrub with multiple stems arising from the base, with branches that feel somewhat brittle and break with a sharp snap

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are small, brownish, and pointed, arranged in opposite pairs along the smooth gray-brown twigs

habitat: As an ornamental species, Wright viburnum is found in cultivated settings like suburban gardens, parks, and landscape plantings throughout New England. It occasionally escapes cultivation and can establish in woodland edges and disturbed areas. This adaptable shrub tolerates various soil conditions but prefers well-drained sites in partial shade to full sun.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in early May, followed by showy white flower clusters in late May that buzz with pollinator activity.
seasonality.summer: Lush green foliage provides dense coverage while bright red berries begin forming and ripening through late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant shades of red, orange, and purple while berries ripen to glossy black, creating a spectacular autumn display.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the shrub's open structure, with small pointed buds and persistent berry stems marking last year's fruit clusters.

funFact: Wright viburnum berries change color like a traffic light in reverse - starting green, turning bright red, then finally ripening to black, with all three colors often visible on the same cluster simultaneously in early fall!
confusionNotes: Wright viburnum can be confused with other ornamental viburnums, but its distinctly ribbed leaves with parallel veins running straight to the leaf edges set it apart from most relatives. The red-to-black berry progression is also distinctive among cultivated viburnums.
contextualKnowledge: While Wright viburnum is not native to New England, it's become a common landscape plant that occasionally escapes cultivation. Gardeners should be aware that this Asian species may self-seed in favorable conditions, though it's not currently considered invasive in the region.
compareHints: Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change. Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with its three-lobed leaves, Wright viburnum has simple oval leaves with very prominent parallel veining.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
